<security_assessment>
<decision>SAFE</decision>
<details>
This pacman hook is a standard post-transaction hook that restarts the `vicinae.service` user unit for all logged-in users after the package is upgraded. The command iterates over user sessions using `loginctl list-users`, then checks if the service is enabled for each user with `systemctl --user is-enabled`, and restarts it if so. This is a common and expected pattern for packages that install systemd user services, ensuring the updated service takes effect immediately. There is no obfuscation, no network activity, no unexpected file operations, and no departure from normal packaging practices. </details>

LLM auditresponse for PKGBUILD:
<security_assessment>
<decision>SAFE</decision>
<details>
This PKGBUILD for the vicinae package follows standard AUR packaging practices. The main source is fetched from the project's own GitHub repository (https://github.com/vicinaehq/vicinae) as a pinned tarball with a verified sha256sum. A local pacman hook file is also included as a source with a pinned checksum.

The `prepare()` function uses `curl` to call the GitHub API (`api.github.com`) for the project's own repository to retrieve the commit SHA behind the annotated tag. This is a common and reasonable pattern to obtain the actual commit hash for build-time metadata, since `git archive` tarballs don't include commit information. The fetched JSON is saved to a file and then parsed with `jq` to extract the commit SHA — the content is never executed, only used as a string in a cmake variable. The cmake build itself is standard, and the package install routine uses the normal `cmake --install` flow into `$pkgdir`.

There is no evidence of obfuscated code, encoded payloads, data exfiltration, backdoors, or execution of remotely-fetched code. The only network operation beyond the declared source download is a read-only API call to GitHub for the same project, which is an ordinary and expected pattern.
</details>

LLM auditresponse for vicinae.install:
<security_assessment>
<decision>SAFE</decision>
<details>
This is a standard `vicinae.install` post-install script for the vicinae launcher/snippet tool. The `post_install()` function performs two operations consistent with the application's stated purpose of input device monitoring and input injection for snippet expansion:

1. **`setcap "cap_dac_override+ep"`**: Grants the `cap_dac_override` capability to the `vicinae-input-server` helper binary. This is an unusually broad capability (it bypasses all DAC permission checks, effectively allowing the process to read/write any file), but it is being applied to the package's own helper binary for the documented purpose of accessing `/dev/input/eventXX` devices. A more minimal approach (e.g., adding the user to the `input` group, or using a narrower capability like `cap_dac_read_search`) would be preferable from a least-privilege standpoint, but this is a packaging/configuration decision, not evidence of injected malicious code.

2. **`modprobe uinput`**: Loads the `uinput` kernel module required for input injection, with appropriate fallback error handling. The comment also notes that since v0.20.3 a `modules-load.d/vicinae.conf` file is installed for persistence across reboots, which is the proper systemd/loadable-module approach.

No network requests, obfuscated code, data exfiltration, unexpected downloads, or other supply-chain attack indicators are present. This is normal upstream packaging behavior.
</details>
<evidence>
</evidence>
<summary>Standard post-install script for input device access</summary>
</security_assessment>
